inline.s: Ming Xi

blocks.text: 30. A Peaceful Passing

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Qian Bingjun Sees the Land of Ultimate Bliss and Is Assisted in Reciting the Buddha’s Name at Death)

Qian Bingjun, courtesy name Hengfu, was a man of Nantong. He lost both parents in childhood, and was by nature simple, sincere, and filial. Growing up, he entered school, mastered letters, and then went to Luzhou to study machinery. He once worked at the Dasheng No. 2 Mill, and later became director of the Gongfu Electric Light Plant of the Reclamation and Herding Company, also serving as a staff member of the company; it was thus that I came to know him. In his dealings with others, he remained respectful even after long acquaintance. In managing his livelihood he worked diligently and spent frugally, and his family thereby attained modest comfort. In

, in June he fell ill with a throat ailment. The doctors were of no avail, and he was in grave danger. On the urging of a good friend he constantly drank Great Compassion water, and his illness gradually healed. From this, seeds from former lives were perfumed and awakened within him; he took refuge in the Buddha and adopted a vegetarian diet, fixing a daily course of Buddha-recitation. Later he went to Suzhou and took refuge with Master Yinguang, the Thirteenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, who gave him the name Huishi. From then on his views grew ever more correct, and he recited the Buddha’s name with greater diligence. In matters of the Buddhadharma he shrank from no toil and feared no difficulty, and did all he could to bring them to accomplishment.

In the end, called forth by former karma and brought on by toil, his lung disease grew worse day by day. Though medical treatment was of no avail, he never ceased reciting the Buddha’s name. In the last ten days or so before his death, I invited Master Xinjing and several laymen such as Xi Chaozai to take turns reciting the Buddha’s name daily. If his allotted span were not yet exhausted, we would seek to avert calamity and prolong his life; if his allotted span were already exhausted, we would assist him in reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth. Through the Buddha’s response, he indeed enjoyed a spell of excellent spirits. He said: I saw my teacher, Master Yinguang, and I saw the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, with all its adornments and all its radiance; from that time my mind opened ever wider. He told people, “Even if I did not recite the Buddha’s name, I would not much cling to worldly affairs — how much the less, then, as one who does recite it.” He also gave instructions concerning the family affairs to follow his death, arranging them in the greatest detail. On the evening two days before the Double Ninth of this year, I suddenly heard that the layman’s illness had turned critical and that he was calling for me to assist in recitation; but because communications were cut off, neither Master Xinjing nor I could get there. Fortunately his wife, Madam Peng, who also kept a lifelong vegetarian diet and honored the Buddha, led the children and the household in reciting the Buddha’s name for him, and the layman passed away peacefully. The next day, hearing the news of his death, I went to inquire how he had been at the end. They told me that his family had all been able to help by reciting the Buddha’s name, that they had restrained their tears and wept only silently, and that there were no particular auspicious signs. In my humble opinion, if at the moment the layman relinquished his retribution his family could refrain from weeping and help him by reciting the Buddha’s name, then thoughts of affection would not arise and right mindfulness would be clear of itself; although there were no remarkable auspicious signs, by this cause and condition he may, I believe, have attained rebirth. The layman lived fifty-two years, born at the hour of the dragon on the seventh day of the first month, and died in
, on the seventh day of the ninth month, at the hour of the rooster. I am ashamed that I have no literary talent, and being by nature remiss, I have been late in writing this record for him.
Xing Deheng

blocks.text: 31. Seeing the Lotus and Attaining Rebirth

inline.s: (Original title: Yong Guiping, Sincere in His New Faith, Sees the Lotus at Death and Attains Rebirth)

Mr. Yong Guiping was a man of Yongjia Town in Hanshan County, Anhui. His family was poor and he did not finish his schooling. At twenty he gave up study for business. Through the help of his maternal uncle he was recommended to an egg factory in northern Anhui as an accountant. As he was quite capable, he was soon promoted to manager. It happened that the First World War broke out, business prospered abnormally, and the family fortunes grew steadily more ample. His first wife bore two daughters, both of whom were married off in turn. After this upheaval he moved to Wuhu.

Because the times were troubled and his dwelling never at peace, he had often heard that Guanyin’s responses are inconceivable and that reciting the Guanyin Sutra can avert disaster; and so he recited it daily, praying for the removal of his karmic obstacles. Later, through frequent visits with Cui Siqiao, the son-in-law of his friend Mr. Wang, he first heard the Buddhadharma. Layman Cui urged him to cultivate the Pure Land practice alone, whereby one may forever escape the sea of suffering: with deep faith and earnest vows, holding the Name and reciting the Buddha’s name, one will surely at the end be received by the Buddha and reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there to enjoy immeasurable bliss. At first hearing, Yong could not believe or understand it, thinking that Buddha-recitation was the doing of foolish men and women, and that the Land of Ultimate Bliss was no more than an expedient teaching of the Buddha. Later, after Layman Cui had gently and patiently opened his understanding, he questioned him again, saying: Do you know whether the Saha world truly exists? This Saha world is in fact amassed by the deluded karmic power of living beings. Since the deluded karmic power of living beings can conjure a world out of nothing, then Amitabha Buddha, perfect in immeasurable merit, amassing a Land of Ultimate Bliss by the power of his great compassionate vow, should be all the more certainly believed without doubt. Hearing this, Yong’s faith and understanding opened at once. Layman Cui also gave him the Ten Essentials of the Pure Land to read and recite. From then on he studied with ardor, utterly unlike his former self, keeping the ten fast days each month and reciting the Buddha’s name single-mindedly morning and evening, vowing to be born in the West.

Who would have thought that at the beginning of the eleventh month of that winter he suddenly fell ill and could not rise; medicine and physicians were of no avail, so he summoned no more doctors and simply recited the Buddha’s name with one mind. He said to his wife: Now I recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly, and I have no pain; moreover, I have a good place to go. Hearing this, his wife wept without ceasing. Yong said: “I am not dying now — I am only moving to another place. It is as if this house were already ruined and one moved elsewhere to live; why grieve? Your weeping now makes my worldly feelings grow; if through this I were to fall, how could your heart bear it?” He added: I once heard people speak of the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation and could never bring myself to believe it. This autumn, in

, in the seventh month, thanks to Layman Cui’s guidance, he brought me to believe, accept, and practice it; I am endlessly grateful to him. Then, early the next morning, he urgently instructed his family: On my behalf, go to Old Master Xinyan of Gongdelin and seek refuge. When the refuge certificate arrived, he held it and read it through once, showing great joy. He then asked his family to support him to sit facing west, and told them all to assist in recitation together. Before long he said joyfully: A lotus flower has already appeared before me — I shall certainly be born in the West. His wife said to him: You have only resolved on this for a few months — how have you reached such a state? Yong said: This is not something you women can know. In practice, sincerity and unremitting effort are what matter; why speak of whether the time was long or short? It is well that you have kept a vegetarian diet for many years; (pointing at his wife) if you can recite the Buddha’s name with one mind, in the future you will surely meet me in the West. I may be able to come and deliver you — that too is not impossible. Having spoken, he still sat upright, palms joined, reciting the Buddha’s name, until at midday he passed away. More than ten hours later, when his body was encoffined, his face was as in life, his four limbs soft, and the crown of his head still warm.
Fo Long

blocks.text: 32. Both Reborn Together

inline.s: (Original title: The Parents of Layman Chen Xiangquan Pass Away at Ease on the Same Day)

My mother, of the Wan family, taboo name Weiyi, style name Shigu, was originally from Tianmen in Hubei, and moved to Bingkeng, a place eight li from Huangpen Town across the river from Anqing. In youth she received her family’s teaching, was well versed in the rites, and was gifted with intelligence; she was the third and youngest daughter, the most beloved of my maternal grandfather. My grandfather loved the Buddha all his life, and so my mother, taught by him, believed in the Buddha from childhood.

At eighteen my mother married my father, and bore five sons and four daughters; in rearing her children she spared herself no toil, and in keeping herself and managing the household she was upright, frugal, and sparing.

My late father, of the Fu family, style name Zhigong, taboo name Shaolan, was the eldest son of my grandfather Weibin. His original home was Sanqiao Town in the western countryside of Anqing; because my grandfather carried on business in Shanghai, the family lodged there for nearly a hundred years. As there were many children, the burden of livelihood was not easy, and added to this were frequent moves and a life of drifting uncertainty; so the children could not be sent to school, and all the books my brothers and sisters read were what we gained at home under my mother’s goading and instruction.

My mother was most devout in serving the Buddha. Though life was unsettled, the dwelling narrow and unclean, and the household chores heavy and toilsome, yet morning and evening she reverently bowed and burned incense before the holy image of Guanyin and silently recited the name of Bodhisattva Guanyin, and never once did she let a day pass without doing so.

When the Shanghai War broke out on August 13, my father happened to be in Hong Kong and had not returned (at that time our family lived at Laoximen in the southern city of Shanghai). Amid the panic of gunfire all day and unending rifle shots, when all the neighbors had fled and left the place empty, my mother could still sit calmly cross-legged, reciting the holy names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, fearing nothing. So firm was her resolve in the Way.
, in 1940 my mother redoubled her diligence, striving bitterly in the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation. Every day she rose at dawn, lit the oil lamps

, and in reverent attire went before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to bow and make offerings, to plead and repent, closing her eyes and joining her palms, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Amitabha Sutra, the Universal Gateway Chapter, the Ksitigarbha Sutra, the Heart Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, the White-Robed Divine Mantra, the Cundi Mantra, and others, practicing as taught. From 40 until 43
when she passed away, throughout these four years her heart of utmost sincerity, her profound heart, and her heart of dedication and vow
surpassed even what they had been before. In her spirit of vigor and valor, even in bitter winter or sweltering heat she would never consent to slacken for a moment.

Though my mother never fully received the precepts in her life, on the second, sixth, and ninth months and on the new and full moon days and the birthdays of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas she kept the fast. Whenever she saw a neighbor kill a chicken or a duck, she would join her palms toward it and recite the Buddha’s name, or recite the Rebirth Mantra, praying for its deliverance. Even at the sight of an insect or a mosquito in danger, she would always find some way to save it.
41, when the cost of living in Shanghai soared and it grew hard to make a living there, she accompanied my parents back to the old home, lodging at Bailin Yangya House in Yanshan Township, Anqing.

My late father had originally no faith in Buddhism. Seeing my mother recite the Buddha’s name and bow to the Buddha, he neither slandered nor hindered her. My mother then urged him to recite the Buddha’s name exclusively — with such sincerity, letting the sound continue unbroken, so that no thought should pass in vain; it is simple and easy to practice. From then on, whenever my mother recited, my father would recite aloud along with her. And so my parents would often sit facing each other, talking and laughing: “When I go to the West, I shall surely take you with me.”

, in mid-August (that is, half a month before her death), my father suddenly said: “I dreamed of a golden man with a red face standing before me.” My mother also said: “In the night I dreamed that three monks came into our house, shaved my head and gave me the precepts for me, and then told me to set out.” With that my mother woke with a start. Three days later my father fell ill, and my mother too felt slightly unwell. So she said to Peiqing with a smile: “Tomorrow I shall take your father out, one before the other, to look at the mountain scenery.” She also said: “After I am gone, do not weep, I beg you. If you weep, you will make me feel heavy and miserable all over. If you recite the Buddha’s name, I shall feel light in body, peaceful and free of trouble.” At the same time she took out all the deeds, contracts, notes, and account books for the farmland and handed them over to Peiqing, instructing him: “You must not lose these. When your brothers come home, hand them over to them.”

On the day of her death, my father said: “My illness is already better. Daughter, you may add more oil to the lamp in my room; wait a little, then come and see me again — tomorrow I shall be able to go out.” After a short while my father had already departed this life. My elder sister felt her heart cut as with a knife, so grieved she wished not to live; yet still she dared not wail aloud. My mother, in another room, suddenly said with a laugh: “How is your father?” She answered: “Father is already better.” She asked again: “Which direction is the West?” Then she said: “There are too many people in the room, too much noise and confusion.” And again: “Daughter! If not now, when will you recite the Buddha’s name to aid my return to the West? Do not grieve; recite the Buddha’s name quickly, and when I have gone far you may mourn as much as you like.” Having spoken, she closed her eyes and sat cross-legged. My elder sister assisted in recitation at her side, and my mother, smiling, passed away seated at ease. At that time my father’s body was not yet cold, and my compassionate mother had gone with him to the West.

My father lived fifty-seven years and my mother fifty-eight. It is a pity that our home village was then in a region surrounded and watched by the enemy and the puppet forces, where human affairs were tangled and conditions harsh; none of us brothers could hurry back to see them off to rebirth in the West in person. This is a lifelong regret.
Chen Xiangquan

blocks.text: 33. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Shen Zhifen Bids Farewell by Letter, to Meet Again in the Land of Lotuses)

Layman Shen, taboo name Youlie, style name Bowei; Zhifen was his Dharma name. He was by nature generous and kind, never tiring of doing good. Fond of the Buddhadharma, he kept the Diamond Sutra for more than twenty years. Then, six years ago, he met in Shanghai the venerable Chen Wuwo and Layman Chen Hailiang, who gave him Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings to read; only then did he know that the Dharma gate of the Pure Land can transcend the three realms crosswise and bring accomplishment in this very life. He resolutely gave rise to faith, asked Layman Hailiang to seek the three refuges from Master Desen, and, lodging in Shanghai, firmly resolved in faith and earnestly cultivated the Pure Land practice. He bowed and recited, diligent without slackening, and kept a lifelong vegetarian diet. When guests came, his talk was of nothing but the propagation of the Pure Land, or the responsive traces of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he touched on no other matters. Because of this, very many people gave rise to faith and took up the practice of Buddha-recitation. The layman practiced himself and transformed others; his heart for spreading the Way was urgent. He once said that if the times should become peaceful, he would invite fellow practitioners to found a Lotus Society on Mount Lu, as a means of leadership. How earnest was the layman’s vow-power! When the War of Resistance was won and communications between Shanghai and Hankou were restored, the layman’s worthy son (that is, the layman’s son; “worthy son” is an honorific for another’s son), Layman Huiqing, brought him to Hankou to care for him. The whole way, devastation met his eyes on every side, and he was deeply moved to sorrow; he vowed to be born early in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and then to return quickly to the Saha world to save living beings far and wide. After arriving in Hankou he bowed and recited all the more earnestly in his lodging. Every Sunday he would go to the Wuhan branch of the Permanent Memorial Society of Master Yinguang, where, under the guidance of Master Yuanche, he cultivated together with fellow Lotus friends.
This year (

1946) in the third month, a slight illness lingered, his food and drink gradually diminished, and his emaciation increased day by day; yet he still did not relax his Buddha-recitation in the slightest. Once in a while he would rise and sit a little, and when he could not hold up he would lie down again. In the sixth lunar month, because his room was narrow and painfully hot, a sedan chair was prepared and he moved to the Qingji Pure Temple. There the buildings were spacious and his body and mind were somewhat eased. Moreover he constantly heard the sound of the Buddha’s name, which sustained his right mindfulness. For this temple was a place in Hankou devoted exclusively to the cultivation of the Pure Land. After he had stayed in the temple a long while, his illness showed no worsening, but his food and drink grew ever less. Yet he could still rise and sit for a short while. From
July

onward he suddenly stopped eating and drinking, and only occasionally sipped a little warm boiled water. Knowing that the time of his rebirth was near, he urgently asked the temple’s monks to take turns assisting in recitation. He also asked for paper and brush, and wrote a letter from his sickbed bidding farewell to his fellow practitioners in Shanghai and to his fellow townsman the venerable Layman Fu Yongyan, in which were the words, “Soon I shall go west before my elder brother; from now on we shall meet again in the Land of Lotuses.” During his illness Master Desen and Layman Chen Hailiang sent letters from Suzhou and Shanghai spurring him on all the more, earnestly urging him not to let the karmic cause of Buddha-recitation go to waste. He was further favored by Master Yuanche and the venerable Layman Fang Deren, who came often to his sickbed and told him to put down all ten thousand ties and press single-mindedly toward the West. The layman joyfully accepted it all, and his resolve to seek rebirth in the West grew firmer still. Once he saw a great white light in his room. Through these ten days and nights the sound of assisting recitation never broke, and the layman could still sometimes recite along with the assembly. For the last three days before his death he said not a single word. On the third day of the eighth month, at a quarter past eleven at night, he suddenly said, “I am going,” and after that had no more words, though his lips still moved slightly. After a while they stopped, and he lay in the auspicious posture and passed peacefully to the West. To the very end his consciousness was clear. Some hours later Master Yuanche tested him, and the crown of his head was still warm. Fourteen hours afterward he was placed in the jar, seated cross-legged; his body was soft as cotton and his face as in life. All who saw or heard of it praised him with one voice: without doubt he was reborn in the Pure Land. He lived sixty-nine years.
Peng Guanghong

blocks.text: 34. Taking Leave of His Mother Before Rebirth

inline.s: (Original title: The Boy Gong Zaiming Sees Amitabha and Takes Leave of His Mother Before Rebirth)

The boy Gong Zaiming was the grandson of the venerable Layman Gong Zongyuan, a pioneer of Buddhist studies in Jiangyin. On the day of his birth someone brought a gilded bronze image of Amitabha Buddha, and his mother was the first to open the wrapping and see the image; that night she gave birth. At his full month it happened to be the day of Shakyamuni’s attainment of the Way. He was then only eleven years old, with a straight nose and square mouth, of dignified appearance. The year before last he took refuge with Master Huisan, who gave him the name Fajian, and he kept the six fast days. His grandfather taught him all manner of sutras, mantras, and praises, and he was tireless in his diligence. The Great Compassion Mantra, the Universal Gateway Chapter, and the Heart Sutra he could all recite from memory. His voice was resonant and mature, and he could raise the gong and lead the assembly. Last year his family held a forty-nine-day Guanyin vow for world peace, and though he was weak, he would not break off from it. He loved cleanliness by nature: his clothes and shoes, though old, were never soiled, and the things he arranged were orderly in every detail. His books and writing materials never wore out through the years. He had perseverance: when his grandfather told him to light the incense coil and the lying incense each morning, he did not stop even when ill.

Sadly, last summer he fell ill with alternating chills and fever; medicine and physicians were of no avail, and in the end he could not be saved. In his illness he did not forget to recite the Buddha’s name. He asked his mother for his prayer beads; too weak to work them with his fingers, he hung them on the bed canopy hook. When his illness turned critical and his mother sobbed aloud, he said, “Son is all right — why cry?” When his belly hurt, he would call on his mother to recite the Great Compassion Mantra. On the eve of his death his eyes were bright, gazing outward. His mother asked what he was doing. He answered: Looking at Amitabha Buddha. Seeing this, his mother knew there was no hope of his living, and with tears she said, “My son is about to be reborn — what am I to do?” He answered: You may bring my elder sister home to keep me company (his sister was then studying at Qinchuan). She also asked what he wished to wear after death, and he answered that he wanted to wear a monk’s robe. His mother said, “Can you wear the newly knitted woolen hat?”
He shook his head and said: I want a monk’s hat. His mother said

, “Do you want the prayer beads?” He answered: I have none of my own. (In truth his heart desired his mother’s copper-ringed beads — mere childishness.) His mother said, “Shall I give you mine?” Only then did he nod. His mother went on, “There are still many Western-style suits — to whom shall they go?” He answered: You may give them to younger brother Zhong (one year younger than he, whom everyone took for his twin). His mother said, “What of the many toys and things you use?” He answered: Give them to whomever you please. By now he already knew well that he would not rise again, and had let go of every thought. So the whole family assisted him in recitation, and the sound of the wooden fish and gong never ceased. Hearing it, he seemed quite at ease, and now and then asked for boiled water. It drew on into the deep of night, and his breath gradually grew faint; amid the sound of the great assembly reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away peacefully. Some hours later they washed his body: his limbs were soft and his face still warm. When he was encoffined his features were as in life, and all who saw him marveled. Most marvelous of all, this child was born and died on the same day of the year, the eighth of the eleventh month. In childhood he believed in the Buddha, sincere and unremitting. At death his mind was clear, his body free of suffering, and his heart free of clinging. Judged by the sutras and treatises, this is proof enough that he was born in the West beyond doubt.
Zhi Ming

blocks.text: 35. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Fu Huikuan Burns Incense and Bows, Recites the Buddha’s Name, and Is Born in the West)

The layman’s surname was Fu, his given name Zhihong; Huikuan was his Dharma name. His original home was Dinghai in Ningbo, and he had lived abroad in Shanghai for many years. He had long possessed good roots and had believed in the Buddha since childhood. At twenty-nine he fell gravely ill, and in his delirium his spirit wandered to the Xiahai Temple in Hongkou, where he saw all manner of retribution for good and evil; when he recovered, his resolve to believe in the Buddha grew firmer still. In the third month of his fifty-seventh year he was again stricken with apoplexy: his mouth could not speak and his feet could not walk, so he lay in bed while all the physicians were at a loss. One day at noon he pointed with his hand for the window to be opened; the family, following the doctor’s orders, paid no heed. The layman then struck the bed and asked for a brush, and wrote the two characters “Guanyin.” Only then did the family understand that the Great One had come in radiance, and they opened the window and knelt to receive him; at once a rare fragrance struck the nose. The layman opened his mouth and asked for boiled water, appearing to swallow a elixir, and joined his palms as if in thanks; and from this the illness turned from grave to better, though he still could not speak or walk. That summer the layman vowed to go on pilgrimage to Mount Putuo to repay the Great One’s vast grace. His family and physicians tried in vain to dissuade him, and so his sons accompanied him there. They set out on the fourth day of the sixth month, and reached Putuo the next morning. While resting and drinking tea in the great hall of the Ciyun Hermitage, he felt a strange itch in his throat and coughed up several mouthfuls of thick phlegm; suddenly he could speak, though not clearly, and his feet could actually walk alone, supporting themselves against the wall. His joy and relief were beyond measure; and so he reverently bowed to the Three Jewels and gave thanks for the compassionate grace. After staying ten days he returned to Shanghai, took refuge with the venerable Master Xingci, and bowed and recited with ever greater diligence.
This year (

1948) on the tenth day of the sixth month, at about four in the afternoon, he told his family to summon a barber. After his hair was cut he washed himself, and said to the barber: “Today I must put on a show.” He then walked around the house inspecting it, and told them to sweep and clean it. Seeing that the household had hired a tailor to make clothes of red and green, he said: “What are you making those for? Your big business is coming.” When he had returned to his room he chatted and laughed with the servants as usual. At about five o’clock he said, “Until we meet again,” and having sent the servants out of the room, he went alone into the Buddha hall, burned incense, and bowed. When the bowing was done he sat cross-legged on the sofa and recited the holy name of Amitabha. When the family invited him to take tea and cakes, they saw that he made no answer, sitting upright as though deep in meditative absorption; only then did they know that he had thus relinquished his retribution and returned to the West. The ancients said: “Where affection is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world; where thought is not single, one is not born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.” As for this layman, with so great a household and children and grandchildren in numbers, at the end he did not cling to love and affection, but cut his hair and washed, and sat serenely free. When we consider that he said to the tailor, “The big business is coming,” he was showing that the family’s mourning garments were soon to be made; and when he said to the servants, “Until we meet again,” that was the voice of final parting. He seemed to know in advance that his time had come — had he not long possessed great good roots, merit, and karmic causes, how could he have been so serene and free? Alas! Auspicious signs at rebirth such as this layman’s — I have seldom seen their like!
You Youwei

blocks.text: 36. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Old Farmer Lu Genxiang — “I Am About to Be Born in the West; Come and Assist My Recitation”)

Lu Genxiang was a man of Lu Village, southeast of Yunting Town in the eastern countryside of Jiangyin. He worked as a farmer and was unlettered, but thoroughly honest and sincere. Ordinarily he believed in cause and effect and loved to recite the Buddha’s name. From

1944, when the Yunguang Lotus Society was founded at Yunting, Genxiang joined the society, and from then on kept a lifelong vegetarian diet. By day he went about his old work of farming, and in the evening he recited the Buddha’s name for the time of one stick of incense as his regular course. Beyond that, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the Buddha’s name never left his lips or his mind.

On the fifth day of the twelfth month, in the bingxu year, Genxiang, now seventy-two, returned from weeding the wheat field feeling slightly unwell. He said to his wife: “I am about to be born in the West,
you may invite people to assist my recitation for me”

His wife, seeing him as hale as ever, suspected it was said in jest, and did not respond. Genxiang went into his room by himself, took out the burial clothes he had prepared in advance, and, finding pockets in them, tore them all out, saying: “I am going to be born in the West; I shall have no use for coin and paper money, so these pockets are not needed.” When that was done he changed his clothes himself, and was wholly new from head to foot. His wife felt that something was strange, and sent people to summon his three sons home. The eldest son worked in shipping at Wuxi, and the round trip took two days. Genxiang stopped his wife, saying: “The hour of my rebirth has come; I cannot wait long. There is no point in the boys coming home — I am about to go.” He also instructed her: “After I have gone, do not weep; only recite the Buddha’s name for me a good deal. It is quite all right to recite it at the society.” When he had finished speaking, he recited the Buddha’s name himself, calm as always, and within a quarter of an hour he passed away peacefully, sitting upright. His mind was clear and bright, and he had no suffering of illness at all.
Xiao Zhen

blocks.text: 37. A Rare Fragrance in the Air

inline.s: (Original title: The Child Pan Liangcai Is Born in the West Amid a Rich and Wondrous Fragrance)

In Cixi County there was a “Private Cidong Home for the Old and Young,” founded by the retired old monk Haoming of the Jingyuan Temple together with several great benefactors of Shanghai, which had always taken in more than a hundred old people and children who had no one to depend on. Each day, besides attending classes as in an ordinary public school, at night a teacher led them in reciting the Buddha’s name for the time of one stick of incense, to repent their karmic obstacles for them and nurture their merit and wisdom, so as to form good habits in them and make them good citizens in the future.
Among them was a child named Pan Liangcai. This year (

1947) he was just twelve. He had been begging in the neighboring villages, and one day, in a certain roadside pavilion, it happened that Director Hao passed by. Seeing him small and pitiable, he took him in at the home. But he had a sore on his buttock that had rotted into a hole, so that he could only walk with slow steps. Yet though he bore this ailment, he was well disciplined in the home; every day, besides listening to the teacher’s lessons, in his free time he recited the Buddha’s name with great earnestness, and whenever the time for recitation came he was ready and waiting long before. Because of the sore on his buttock he could not walk easily, and when the others walked around reciting the Buddha’s name, he only stood to one side with his palms joined, following along aloud, sound by sound.

This time, at the beginning of the fourth month, he suddenly fell ill and could not leave his bed. Though he was treated, the medicine never took effect. He lay in the sickroom, and his tea and water and his calls of nature were attended to in turn by the matron and a few of the students. Later, because from the hole of his sore excrement often leaked out, and because of the stench, the matron and the students were no longer willing to attend him; and so the director moved him into his own thatched hut, assigned others to look after him, and often advised him to recite the Buddha’s name well, saying that even if his illness did not mend and he died, he would still, by the Buddha’s compassionate power, be received and guided to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. He listened well to the director’s words, and in his illness still recited the Buddha’s name without break. Later, when the director went to Ningbo on the home’s business, he too returned to the home for the old and young. Not many days after his return his illness gradually grew worse. On the thirteenth, when the teacher Mr. Lu Ren saw that he was at the point of death, he at once gathered many of the students to recite the Buddha’s name with him, and taught him to recite it himself as well. Though he had reached the final crisis, his mind was still very clear and he could still reciting the Buddha’s name; even at the very moment of death his lips kept moving slightly, so one knew that he was still reciting. While the great assembly was reciting, a fragrance suddenly filled the room, exceedingly rich and fragrant, and lasted for the space of an hour. This room had been very foul; because of the recitation a rare fragrance was evoked, and everyone marveled and cried out in wonder. Even as they marveled, the child, seizing the moment when the fragrance was at its richest, breathed his last and was born in the West.
Chang Zhi

blocks.text: 38. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Liu Qichang Arranges His Own Funeral Affairs and Beats Time While Reciting the Buddha’s Name)

Liu Qichang, courtesy name Yukun, was a man of Yaoshan in Hebei. He was by nature brilliant and had learning and conduct. Reading Master Huiyuan’s Collected Writings, he could understand them all; reading Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings, he praised them without end, and could recite many of their chapters and passages and relate them to others. Apart from his formal daily course of recitation aloud with bowing, at other times he only recited the Buddha’s name silently. Yet in his conduct, in small matters and fine points of behavior, he was far from strict. In earlier years gambling and drinking were unavoidable for him. Only in the past year did he give them up entirely, and he would not even smoke tobacco. It was only in the great essentials that he was wholly sincere and earnest. His father died early, and he served his widowed mother, of the Yang family, with the utmost filial devotion. In life he provided for her, and in death he buried her; in every matter he was sure to be sincere and complete. When his elder cousin Liu Rongchang was falsely accused and imprisoned, he beat the official court drum to rescue him, and moved the county magistrate to release his cousin, and the magistrate himself wrote the four large characters “Filial and Fraternal, a Model to Follow” to commend him. Toward his teacher he was reverent and provided for him; when the teacher died, he looked after his family. Toward relatives and friends he had especially many excellent deeds. Several of his cousins’ daughters, whose parents had died and left no heirs, he kept in contact with, giving them cotton and sundry goods each year without the least stinting. With classmates and friends he was as good as his word, worth a thousand pieces of gold. Meeting with the poor and the afflicted, he did not grudge wealth or treasure, but did all within his heart’s power to rescue them.

Before his death he often told his family: In all my life I have not failed in human relations; I am already seventy-one, and who is there that does not die? I have lived in accord and shall die at peace. Even when I can no longer speak, I shall still silently recite Amitabha; I have no fear, no grief, no attachment. He also said: My illness needs no treatment; my illness will certainly not be cured, and seeking doctors and taking medicine would only waste money to no purpose. His wife, of the He family, consoled him, saying: After the autumn cools, the illness will mend of itself. The layman rebuked her angrily: I look on death as a return home; I do not need you to say pretty things to me. From this one can see that he had long been weary of birth and death and did not wish to dwell long in the Saha world; and so at the end he was calm and at ease, and without the labor of many people assisting his recitation he passed away peacefully.

Since vomiting blood once last winter, the layman had felt his body weaken; he ate as usual but grew somewhat thin. This autumn it worsened, with coughing and phlegm, and his food diminished day by day. In mid-seventh month he could no longer rise. On the fourteenth, Huiyang went specially to urge him on, explaining to him the surpassing excellence of Buddha-recitation and the peace and bliss of rebirth in the West, and telling him of Zhang Wenbing, Wang Lanxin, Li Sixun, Chang Kaixiang, Chang Shutian, and others of our parts — all of them excellent in both character and learning, single-minded in reciting the Buddha’s name — who at death had no suffering and all attained rebirth. How much more should you, brother, whose learning and conduct yield to none of them: if you recite the Buddha’s name with one mind, you will without doubt be born in the West. After this encouragement, his resolve was at once settled and his mind opened. He made an agreement with Huiyang, saying: When I reach the crucial moment, you must come and recite the Buddha’s name for me. Huiyang of course readily agreed, saying: I shall take full responsibility for the recitation at the end; and as for your burial and gravestone, I am willing to complete them for you. Then, reflecting that his family did not believe in the Buddha and fearing there might be interference, he sought out the layman’s eldest son Liu Zhende and explained to him the essentials of attending the end with assisted recitation. On the twenty-third, Huiyang went to the Red Cross in Xingtai; unexpectedly the layman passed away at the hour of wei on the twenty-fourth.

At dusk on the second day of the eighth month Huiyang finally returned. Hearing that the layman’s end had been excellent, he at once sent for his two sons and questioned them about everything. They said: Recently our late father (meaning the layman) recited the Buddha’s name constantly, though still not aloud. On the morning of the twenty-fourth his mind was clearer than ever, as though he had no illness at all. He asked for a mirror to look at his face, and wiped it clean himself with a cloth. He gave instructions for all his funeral affairs, down to the smallest detail, in perfect order, saying that he wanted a simple burial, no family sacrifices, and a coffin prepared quickly. Then he said: When I die, do not weep; I shall certainly be born in the West, and that is a joyful matter. If at that time you cannot hold back your tears, you may leave my side and go elsewhere to weep. At noon he still ate half a bowl of fine noodles, with no pain at all, his mind and breath clear. In the afternoon his tongue suddenly grew clumsy and he could not speak; so he tapped his right arm with his index finger, as if beating a wooden fish, and again moved his lips as if reciting the Buddha’s name. We understood his meaning and hurried to welcome the teacher (meaning Huiyang), not knowing that he had gone to Shunde, and then hurried back to attend him. At that time our mother was dozing on another bed in the same room, half asleep and half awake, and saw three monks standing before her bed in blue monastic robes, all with full, round faces, who then went out. When she rose to look, they were nowhere to be seen. At this time we brothers recited the Buddha’s name together, aiding him toward the West. In a single instant he had relinquished his retribution. There was no phlegm and no gasping; he lay on his right side, his head on his right hand, utterly at peace, and the flies all flew away and did not gather. We recited the Buddha’s name for the time of two sticks of incense, and only when the grave clothes were finished did we wash and wipe him and change his garments; his face was fresh and his limbs were not stiff. Only when we moved him to the bier did we begin to wail. It was already the late afternoon hour, and his whole body was cold, except that the crown of his head was still warm. His countenance was bright and clear; all said it was a rare and beautiful sight. Such were the general circumstances of his end. Huiyang, fearing that his sons might have embellished their words, questioned others separately twice, and what he heard differed in nothing, which proves it true and not false.
Chang Huiyang

blocks.text: 39. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Shu Cifan Sits Cross-Legged, Recites the Buddha’s Name, and Passes Away at Ease)

Shu Cifan was a man of Chengdu. He lost his parents early and was raised to manhood by his aunt. By nature he was bold and chivalrous, prizing righteousness. In the twelfth year of the Republic he made a pilgrimage to Putuo and took refuge under his revered teacher. The master saw him carrying his books tucked under his arm and reproved him, saying: “For one who studies the Buddha, reverence comes first. To slight the Dharma in this way is a grave offense.” He heard it but did not awaken to it, and answered carelessly

Yes.” The master said in a stern voice: “The Buddha’s books should be carried with both hands before you!” He was startled, and bowed in thanks for the compassionate teaching. Afterward he often told others of it, saying that the one shout from the master of the scriptures was like hearing a thunderclap, and benefited him for life.

He prospered in business, yet wore coarse cloth and ate simple food like a poor scholar. Sichuan is a land of many mountains, and travelers mostly go by sedan chair; he held that this was not the Dharma of equality, and walked on foot his whole life. When the Buddhist Studies Society was founded in Chongqing, he served as manager of its distribution office. He founded a Buddha-recitation society, which grew into a flourishing Pure Land practice ground. When his revered teacher passed away to the West and a memorial society was founded in Shanghai, he and two or three comrades organized a branch in Chongqing. In the winter of

his asthma came on, and he had by then lived at the distribution office for more than a year. His sons and daughters gathered around urging him to come home. He laughed and said: “I am going to the West; coming home is fine too. But you must do as I say: no wake, no sutra-chanting rites, everything simple. If you have money to spend, take it and use it for the work of spreading the Dharma and benefiting people, and dedicate it to the West on my behalf. That is far better than a lavish funeral and costly encoffining.” His children all promised to obey. He then set out clearly all the affairs he had handled in his life, saying: “The matters of this life are settled in this life.” Once home, he recited the Buddha’s name with one mind and set his whole heart on the West. This year, on the sixth day of the first month, he suddenly had his hair shaved. At midnight on the seventh he sat cross-legged reciting the Buddha’s name, and passed away at ease.
Honghua Monthly

blocks.text: 40. Passing Away at Ease

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Gong Wuhui Passes Away at Ease Amid the Sound of Assisted Recitation)

Gong Wuhui was a man of Changshu, from a family of long standing. He married a woman of the Zhao family, and both husband and wife took refuge in the Three Jewels. In the spring of the thirty-first year of the Republic he founded the Wuxiu Lotus Society, with recitation morning and evening.
1945, in the summer, he fell ill. On the second day of the seventh month, amid the sound of assisted recitation, he passed peacefully to the West. He was forty-two.

blocks.text: 41. Passing Away at Ease

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Lu Huigen Passes Away at Ease Amid the Sound of Assisted Recitation)

Lu Huigen was a man of Kunshan. Filial and fraternal, honest and sincere, he was frugal in his own living. After taking refuge with his revered teacher, he set his heart earnestly on the Land of Peace and Nourishment. Together with Layman Zhu Huijing he founded the Jinxiu Lotus Society, and gave no further thought to any worldly affair. This spring he fell ill, and on the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month he passed to the West amid the sound of assisted recitation. By the earnestness of his ordinary resolve and the single-mindedness of his practice, he gained the condition of assisted recitation at the end; that he was born in the West may be known. He was fifty-eight.

blocks.text: 42. Dissolving Karma and Being Born in the West

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Zhu Huiguan Recites the Buddha’s Name at Death, Dissolves His Karma, and Is Born in the West)

Layman Zhu Mingsan, whose Dharma name was Huiguan, ran an eating house (he made his living by keeping a restaurant). When he heard the Buddhadharma he resolutely gave up the trade (closed the business); though his wife and children might suffer cold and hunger (be frozen and starve), he gave it no thought. He took refuge with Master Desen, practicing himself and transforming others, wholly in accord with Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings. At the canal station in Pi he founded the Faguang Lotus Society. The people of Pi had long heard nothing of the Buddhadharma, and knew nothing at all of the Pure Land Dharma gate; seeing the layman form a society to recite the Buddha’s name, many mocked and jeered at him. The layman practiced the ascetic discipline of patience and gently led them on. In time, those who turned to it in faith gradually grew in number. The layman had been uneducated in youth, but after taking refuge in the Three Jewels, by the sincerity of his faith he stirred up wisdom from former lives, and gradually came to read and recite Buddhist sutras and wholesome books. Whenever he had an insight, he would always put it into practice and use it to exhort others. Having given up his restaurant business, the layman’s livelihood was in sore straits; relying on the help of relatives and friends, he became a petty peddler (a small trader) to keep body and soul together for a time. Even so he stinted his own clothing and food to do deeds that benefited others: buying and releasing living creatures, relieving the poor and the sick, collecting donations on behalf of the memorial society, helping relieve the famine in Henan, and distributing the books of the Honghua Society. In exhorting others and giving relief he was busy from morning to night. There were many heterodox sects in the Pi region, and the layman too had entered the Buddhadharma from a heterodox sect. Yet his views were uniquely correct: one phrase of the Buddha’s name never left his lips, and the thought of rebirth never left his mind. He did good and put away evil, deceiving no one in the dark, and dedicated it all to the Pure Land. He truly practiced the four words “ultimate sincerity and reverence” — even those long in cultivation might not attain to it — and his vow-power for spreading the Dharma was especially earnest. Yet because his family for generations had kept an eating house, his karma of killing was heavy, and he was in the end murdered by bandits. At the end he still recited the Buddha’s name, and when he was encoffined his face was as in life; he must have been able to be born in the West, or perhaps it was heavy retribution lightly borne. Alas! Our district is remote and crude, and the true Dharma is seldom heard. From now on, who will carry on the layman’s great vow and bring benefit and succor to the people of this whole region?
Tang Huigao

blocks.text: 43. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Zhang Xiqi Bathes, Sits Cross-Legged, Recites the Buddha’s Name, and Attains Rebirth)

When I first began to study the Buddha, I most loved to read the scriptures of the prajñā line, using them to cultivate the mind and nurture the nature and to remove affliction. As for the Pure Land school’s rebirth in the West, I used to think it must contain at least a tinge of superstition, and so I once took no very deep interest in writings of the kind of the Biographies of Rebirth and the Records of Rebirth in the West. But recently, because of the marvel of the venerable Layman Zhang Xiqi’s rebirth in the West, I have been unable not to joyfully believe and accept the Pure Land Dharma gate, which covers all three capacities and gathers in both the sharp and the dull. And now I mean to write a record of rebirth in the West — the very kind of writing I once did not care to read — to make a faithful report of the venerable Layman Zhang’s rebirth.

The venerable Layman Zhang Xiqi was a man of Nanxizhang, Xiatang, outside the north gate of Wuxi; he and I are small fellow townsmen of the same county and the same village, and so I know his life very well. In his early years Layman Zhang served in such offices as the Heilongjiang Gold Mining Bureau and the Xicheng Wu Tobacco and Wine Tax Bureau; in middle age he dealt in fruit; and in his later years he suddenly awakened to the impermanence of human life and resolved to study the Buddha. To seek out a true teacher he first went back and forth several times between Hui Mountain and Xi Mountain in Wuxi, and in

he took refuge with Master Juechun of the Zizhu Chan Monastery on Xi Mountain, receiving the Dharma name Changyuan. Afterward he took refuge in turn with Master Shouye of Mount Wutai in Shanxi, Master Pushan of Yuantouzhu in Wuxi, and others. From then on he cultivated the Pure Land Dharma gate with one mind. Each morning he rose at the fifth watch and recited the Shurangama Mantra, the Great Compassion Mantra, the Universal Gateway Chapter of the Lotus Sutra, the Ksitigarbha Sutra, and others; in the evening he recited the Amitabha Sutra and the Heart Sutra. For six or seven years his morning and evening courses never once fell into interruption. At all other free times the Buddha’s name never left his lips, and he often gathered the whole family to recite together; even sitting or lying down he would face west. Whenever he took part in the Dharma assemblies at the Ciyun Hermitage in his home district, Layman Zhang’s voice in reciting the Buddha’s name was especially clear and resonant
Because of Layman Zhang’s utmost sincerity, many villagers were moved by him and took refuge in the Buddha.
In the third month of the thirty-sixth year (

1947) he went to the Jiechuang Monastery in the Western Garden at Suzhou to receive the full upasaka precepts. That winter he said to his wife and children: “I shall not live past this New Year; I am going to the West.” On the eighteenth day of the twelfth month the venerable Layman Zhang suddenly said to his family again: “I am going to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. All of you recite the Buddha’s name before my bed, and on no account weep; if you weep, it will keep me from reaching the West.” Having said this, he burned incense and bathed, then got up on the bed and sat cross-legged. His family gathered around the bed reciting the Buddha’s name, and Layman Zhang recited it himself as well; and amid the resonant sound of the Buddha’s name, Layman Zhang passed away seated in meditation.

As to Layman Zhang’s rebirth, I think there are two points worthy of praise. The first: though Layman Zhang was nearly seventy, he was not ill at all right up to the end, and yet could know in advance the time of his going and pass away seated in meditation at ease. The second: at the end Layman Zhang sat cross-legged with no cushion behind his back or at his sides, and yet right through to the ceasing of his breath his body never moved or fell. I believe Layman Zhang was certainly born in the West — otherwise there could never have been such a marvel. Facts speak louder than eloquence; the story of Layman Zhang’s rebirth far surpasses empty propaganda. From then on those in our district who believe in Buddhism have grown even more eager!
Tang Xiangqing

blocks.text: 44. Seeing the Buddha and Attaining Rebirth

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Liang Shuofu — The West Is Not Far, It Is Right Before Your Eyes)

Layman Liang Shuofu was a man of Xiangtan in Hunan, a graduate of the School of Mines of Oxford University in England. He worked in the insurance business, serving successively as manager of the Taiping Insurance Company in Changsha, Kunming, Hankou, and other places for nearly twenty years. He was kindly and gentle, never speaking or looking in anger, of spotless integrity, extremely frugal in his own living, yet full of pity for the poor and succor for the distressed, giving generously without stint; all who knew him looked up to him. In early years he took refuge with the Vajra Master Nenang Hutuktu to study the esoteric school, and he also revered the Pure Land, keeping a regular course and cultivating without interruption. Every day before the Buddha he would make this vow: “Master, Buddhadharma, and holy Sangha, so long as living beings remain I take refuge; all the sufferings and obscurations of living beings I enter hell to bear in their place; all the roots of good I have gathered in three ages I give wholly to living beings to bring them to Buddhahood; should one fail to attain perfect awakening, may this vow of mine never retreat.” This was the vow-verses the layman composed himself.
In the seventh month of the old calendar of this year (

1948), because of lung cancer he came to Shanghai for treatment at the Zhongshan Hospital. For more than two months he constantly recited the Buddha’s name with one mind, hoping to be born in the Land of Bliss. On the second day of the ninth month he left the hospital and went to the Fuhui Temple at No. 62 Wenlin Road, asking the monks to assist his recitation; his wife, Madam Jin Shoujun, together with his sons Peifu, Peishu, and Peikai, and his son-in-law Shao Yongli, all came to the temple with him. The retreat room of the old Master Daogen was used as the room for assisted recitation, and six monks of the temple were engaged to recite the Buddha’s name in turn without interruption. The family all knelt at his side, earnestly holding the Name. Deep in the night the layman lay with eyes closed; before long he revived, joined his palms, and said, “Amitabha Buddha!” Then with his finger he wrote the two words “the West” in Peishu’s palm and said: “I have just been to the West and have seen Amitabha.” He instructed his family, saying: “Since we are all disciples of the Buddha, everything must follow the Buddha’s rules. After my death my body is to be cremated, and the nanmu coffin must be exchanged for an ordinary one to be burned; for the nanmu coffin is far too costly, and its value could be exchanged for many coffins for the poor to be given in charity.” And so on. (For the Taiping Insurance Company and his colleagues, hearing that the layman was critically ill, had specially contributed a nanmu coffin worth seven thousand gold yuan, to express their respect and condolence.) At noon on the third day the layman again wrote the two words “release life” in Peishu’s palm, and his son at once gave one hundred gold yuan to the old Master Daogen to buy fish and set them free. In the middle of the night that day the layman suddenly said to Peishu: “The West is not far — it is right before your eyes; if you want to see it, you see it!” All in the room who were assisting the recitation, and the family, were deeply moved to hear it. At two in the afternoon of the fourth day the layman suddenly opened his eyes and looked around, saying: “All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have already descended, and the whole room is filled with them.” He repeatedly signaled, as though welcoming them, now joining his palms, now nodding; at last his hands formed the Amitabha mudra and he passed away at ease. At that time the layman’s second daughter, Peiyin, who had received the urgent telegram of her father’s critical illness, had just arrived from Changsha; seeing him, she wailed aloud, and her mother urgently stopped her, saying: “Your father is already born in the West and has escaped the sea of suffering! You need not grieve; you may recite the Buddha’s name with me!” Only then did Peiyin murmur her obedience, throw herself down at her father’s side, and recite the Buddha’s name with utmost earnestness without stopping. On the fifth day the layman’s friend in the Dharma from before his death, Layman Han Dazai, came from Mount Lu and placed a relic of the Vajra Master Nenang Hutuktu into his mouth, gave him the consecration mantra, and prayed that his spirit might be forever firm and leap straight to Buddhahood. At eight in the morning of the sixth day, after the family’s Dharma master had spoken the Dharma, the family and the assembly of monks recited the Buddha’s name all the way as they escorted the body to the Central Funeral Parlor for the full encoffining. When his body was bathed and dressed, it was soft as cotton and his bearing was as in life. His wife, Madam Jin Shoujun, placed a string of amber prayer beads around the layman’s neck and made this wish: “May you accomplish the Buddha Way and save living beings far and wide!” Then Layman Han Dazai recited mantras, made vows, and sprinkled sweet-dew water. The monks and the family still recited the Buddha’s name as they circled the coffin, and after I had spoken the Dharma the coffin was sealed. At nine in the morning of the eleventh day the coffin was again carried to the Jing’an Cemetery for cremation; at eleven the electric fire was lit, and by four in the afternoon, when the ashes were gathered, more than ten teeth were found, along with seven relics the size of beans, bright and translucent as crystal — clear proof of a lifetime of taking refuge in the Buddhadharma and cultivating with utter sincerity. The family now intends to carry the ashes to Mount Lu and build a memorial stupa there, while the teeth and relics will be enshrined separately in a small crystal stupa.
Fu Yan

blocks.text: 45. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Yang Ruikang Sits Upright, Recites the Buddha’s Name, and Passes Away at Ease)

Yang Ruikang was a man of Lüxing Lane in the city of Ningbo. He kept the Xunzhang Silk Shop, and his family was quite well off. Before he was thirty he adopted a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, loved releasing living creatures, and printed and gave away several dozen kinds of scriptures. Later, when the family fortunes declined, he redoubled his good works: whenever he saw anyone in difficulty, he would go so far as to sell his clothes to relieve them. At the age of fifty-one, rising early one day, he arranged the household affairs, bathed and changed his clothes, sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name, and passed away at ease.
Da Mu

blocks.text: 46. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Lü Tongguang Knows the Time in Advance and Writes a Couplet for His Own Mourning)

Lü Tongguang was originally an apprentice in the Xiangkang Clothing Shop on East Main Street in Ningbo. From childhood he kept a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, and he was good at painting Buddha images. At twenty-four his parents wished to get him a wife, but Lü said that his blessings were thin and he dared not burden another; they pressed him and could not prevail, so the matter was dropped. At twenty-seven, in the seventh month, knowing in advance that the time of his death was near, he gave all his savings to help build the Fuju Hermitage. On the thirteenth of that month, after rising in the morning, he bathed and burned incense and recited the Buddha’s name without stopping. At noon the sound ceased; when they looked, his breath had already stopped. On the third day, when he was placed in the coffin, the crown of his head was still warm, and his face wore a smile, his body soft as that of a living man. Before his death Lü had written a couplet for his own mourning: “This brief dust-bound destiny is now ended; / sound upon sound of Buddha-recitation has won rebirth.”

blocks.text: 47. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Hong Tongbai Sees Amitabha and Sits Upright Reciting the Buddha’s Name)

My friend Hong Tongbai was a man of Meicheng Town in Jiande County, Zhejiang. Before Liberation he had served as the town’s magistrate. In his youth he delved into Buddhist principles but did not practice; after Liberation he recited daily at home the Amitabha Sutra, the Diamond Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, and the holy name of Amitabha Buddha. He was honest by nature and warm toward others, delighting in good deeds and in giving, and especially skilled at spreading the Dharma; Lotus friends often gathered at his house to hear him expound the Buddhadharma. He could teach according to the capacities of his listeners and save living beings according to conditions.

1955, in the campaign to eliminate counterrevolutionaries, he was sent to prison, and in prison he still did not cease reciting the Buddha’s name. One day the jailer informed him that he was to be shot the next day. He was not in the least alarmed, and recited the Buddha’s name with one mind the whole night through; the next day, however, the execution was not carried out. Later the same thing happened once more, and by then he had put birth and death entirely outside his mind: he simply lived one day and recited the Buddha’s name one day.

he was released and returned home. Of the three men who had served as town magistrate before him, all had been suppressed; he alone escaped, and he knew in himself that this was the Buddha’s added grace. Therefore he cultivated all the more diligently, and through the six periods of the day and night the Buddha’s name continued unbroken, never leaving his lips and mind.

1964, at the Spring Festival, I went in the morning to pay him a New Year call. He told me that his health had been poor of late. When I asked where he was unwell, he said it was only that his bowels did not move freely and his belly was somewhat bloated. In the middle of the night that day he suddenly called his wife to him and told her: I have already seen Amitabha Buddha; tomorrow he will come to fetch me. If I do not go tomorrow, then I shall have to wait another week. Having said this he put on his clothes, sat cross-legged, and recited the Buddha’s name. His wife, fearing he would take cold in the wintry weather, brought a cap and put it on his head. He said: You go and rest; do not mind me. And with that he took the cap off, sat upright, and recited the Buddha’s name. Seeing that his spirits were very good, his wife paid no attention to what he had said and went to sleep. The next morning she found him with a smile on his face, sitting peacefully and reborn. Many people in the town saw this and marveled at it as something rare, and no few of them came to believe in the Buddha and recite the Buddha’s name because of it.
Told by Zhang Fenggang of the Second Middle School of Yongxiu, Jiangxi; recorded by Yao Nianzhou

blocks.text: 48. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Yan Zhaoyuan Knows the Time in Advance, to the Very Minute)

Yan Zhaoyuan, Dharma name Anji, was originally from Hengren County in Liaoning. He served successively as a normal-school principal and as director of education. After the September 18 Incident he refused the invitations of the Japanese and the puppet regime, moved to Baoqing to settle, and took up Chinese medicine; after Liberation he was director of the Baoqing County Chinese Medicine Hospital and a member of the county’s Political Consultative Conference. He was a firm believer in Buddhism and cultivated the Pure Land practice exclusively, and on
April 26, knowing in advance that his time had come, to the very minute he passed away at ease.

Layman Zhaoyuan was by nature compassionate and kind, loyal and righteous, modest and cautious, and most filial in serving his parents. From childhood he did no evil and practiced every good. In earlier years he was elected chairman of the Morality Society; later, having read the sutras and treatises, he led his whole family to take refuge in the Three Jewels, and then went deep into the scriptural treasury, resolving to keep a vegetarian diet and recite the Buddha’s name. Because he often read Master Yinguang’s Collected Writings, he cultivated the Pure Land Dharma gate exclusively, hoping that in this very life, by the Buddha’s compassionate power, he might be born in the West, escape birth and death, and forever leave the wheel of rebirth.

At fifty-five the layman fell gravely ill. Chinese and Western physicians who examined him concluded that his body could no longer make blood, and that there was no way to cure him. He therefore resigned from the chairmanship of the Chinese Physicians’ Association and other posts and waited for death at home (his family had asked a fortune-teller, who said that his allotted span was already exhausted, and he himself had lost the will to live). When I went to see him, I told him the story of how Yuan Liaofan changed his destiny, and urged him to believe firmly in the Buddhadharma and to be master of his own fate. The layman then gave rise to the great bodhi mind and prayed earnestly

vowing to protect and uphold the Three Jewels and to raise the banner of Dharma in Baoqing County. Before long he dreamed that a great withered old tree had sprouted anew, and someone told him that twenty years had been added to his span.

His illness did indeed take a miraculous turn for the better, and from then on the old layman Yan cultivated with exceptional diligence. He zealously supported the founding of the Anle Temple, and husband and wife cultivated together, never ceasing to bow and recite. At seventy his body weakened and his central energy grew insufficient, so he devoted himself to silently reciting the great Name. It drew on to the fourth month of his seventy-fifth year, and he showed no confusion or inversion at all. He instructed his sons and daughters that at his death there was to be no wailing, no burning of paper money, no accepting of gifts, no changing of clothes or washing; and that they were to wait several hours before touching him. On the morning of the eighteenth of the fourth month his son, daughters, and daughters-in-law saw a light shining from the crown of his head; they discussed it among themselves, not knowing the reason. Presently he asked his niece: “Is the top of my head bright? Has the crown of my head opened?” Not knowing how to answer, his niece asked his daughter, and the daughter, afraid that he would die, answered: “No.” He said: “Then I cannot go this week; you may all go to sleep.” On the twenty-fifth of the fourth month Layman Guozhen came to see him, and he wrote on the box beside him with chalk: “I leave tomorrow; please ask the teacher to come and assist my recitation.” Early on the twenty-sixth he crooked the index finger of his right hand to show everyone the figure nine; no one understood what he meant, so he wrote again with chalk on the box beside him: “Tonight at nine I shall certainly go (be reborn).” At four in the afternoon, when his daughter helped him sit up, he said again that he would certainly go at nine that night. The news quickly spread through the clan and to children and grandchildren and friends and relatives. The younger members of the clan did not believe such a marvel could be, and some came specially to verify it; the west room was packed with people, and from seven or eight o’clock on they kept stealing glances to see what would happen. In the east room there were only his wife, his children, Guozhen, and me, reciting in low voices to assist him. From seven o’clock on he kept asking: “What time is it?” asking every little while; his son Xingjin reported the time to him every fifteen minutes. At eight fifty he asked again; at eight fifty-nine he asked once more, and then passed away at ease — truly one may say he knew the time in advance, to the very minute. Two or three hours after the assisted recitation we changed his clothes; his body was soft. The next day he was encoffined, and the crown of his head was still warm, proving that he had indeed been born in the Western Pure Land. All who were present were shaken, and all who heard were spurred on; the Lotus friends of the whole city were thereby made more diligent, and many people were brought to the Dharma. I witnessed this with my own eyes, and so record it especially, wishing to make it a model of rebirth through Buddha-recitation, and to be born together with Lotus friends everywhere in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Respectfully recorded by Yue Anxing of Baoqing County, Heilongjiang

blocks.text: 49. Foreknowledge of the Time of Departure

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Tao Nengde, His Mind Never Apart from the Buddha, Sits Upright and Is Born in the West)
My father, Layman Tao Shide, whose Dharma name was Nengde,
received the refuges under the old Master Shang Longxia, and in

went to the Ganlu Temple on Mount Ma’an in Ningxia to receive the lay bodhisattva precepts. After taking refuge in the Three Jewels, my father recited the Buddha’s name with one mind each day by the method of the ten recitations, never breaking off. Later he also learned the two periods of daily chanting, and bowed and recited each day; at other times a single phrase of the Buddha’s name was his main practice, and he took no pleasure in worldly talk. In addition he took the five Pure Land sutras, the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra, and other Mahayana scriptures as his auxiliary practice, reciting them with diligence.

he was stricken with illness and pain, and he held to the Buddha’s name all the more diligently. He repeatedly instructed his family and relatives: “When my illness is grave and when I am dying, on no account follow worldly custom by moving me about or weeping. My body is to be cremated; it must not be buried.”

1981, the sixteenth day of the third lunar month, was eleven days before his rebirth. At noon he said to us: “Prepare my funeral affairs; I shall be going soon.” The twenty-fourth, three days before his death, the old Master Shang Longyuan was invited to come. At their first meeting he said only: “In the mind there is only the Buddha; at death one does not part from the Buddha.” The old master nodded again and again and answered: “Amitabha Buddha.” He was already gravely ill, and his lips moved slightly as he continued reciting the Buddha’s name without cease. On the twenty-fifth he sat a while and lay a while, his face serene and his body at ease; one could see no sign of illness in him. At nine o’clock on the twenty-sixth he turned to face west of his own accord and passed away sitting upright, reciting the Buddha’s name. Present at the time were Dharma Master Longyuan, Wang Guojun, Wang Shuyao, Wang Huaiwen, Zhang Quantang, Li Cunyu, Yang Chenglin, Wang Xiushan, Yang Xiulin, and dozens of others, lay believers and good friends who assisted in the recitation. The next day his face was as in life, bright and shining, and all who saw him praised him with reverence and faith. On the fourth day, at the cremation, his limbs were soft and his ashes were many-colored.
His son Hengshu respectfully records it exactly as it was

blocks.text: 50. Single-Mindedness Undisturbed

inline.s: (Original title: Layman Lin Anding Joins His Palms in Farewell at the Buddha-Recitation Assembly)

1984, in the winter, the Pujing Lotus Society at Wolong Mountain in Haoba, Shangyu, Zhejiang, held a consecration Dharma assembly for the three holy ones of the West, and more than forty faithful came specially to the mountain to pay homage. The venerable Layman Lin Anding, who cultivated the Pure Land exclusively on the mountain and was revered by all, suddenly raised his hand in a sign and joined his palms in farewell in the midst of that day’s Buddha-recitation assembly, and afterward passed away at ease. The great assembly was filled with wonder at the sight. The day of Elder Lin’s rebirth was chosen to fall just at the consecration of the three holy ones — precisely so that everyone might see with their own eyes the inconceivable, real trace of the Pure Land Dharma gate. Layman Lin spread the Dharma by his own person, and his merit was surpassing.

Layman Lin Anding was a man of Shaoxing in Zhejiang. In his early years he ran a silk business in Shanghai; after forty he heard a Dharma master of the Yuanming Lecture Hall expound the sutras and came to hear the true Dharma, and sighed: “The Buddhadharma is truly inconceivable!” He at once gave up meat and resolved to study the Buddha, reciting with diligence, and for several decades his daily course was the Lotus Sutra. In recent years he recited the holy name of Amitabha day and night without slackening.

The layman was unstinting in gold for offerings, karmic connections, and charity; and to any who resolved to leave home or to establish a place of practice he gave support with all his strength. Within a few years he gave away his entire well-to-do family fortune.

, in April, at the invitation of the venerable laymen such as Niu Jiuhua of Shangyu, he followed the old tradition of Donglin and founded a Lotus Society at Wolong in Haoba, reciting the Buddha’s name all day long. On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, at the hour of shen, in the midst of the great assembly’s Buddha-recitation, he sat cross-legged, joined his palms, smiled at the assembly, and passed away seated, born in the West. He was eighty-three.

In the month or so before his death, the layman wrote to a certain layman in Hangzhou, saying: “I am now deeply interested in Buddha-recitation, and I want to urge you all to recite the Buddha’s name a great deal too. Bar the three gates firmly: recite clearly and freshly with the mouth, hear clearly and freshly with the ear, and be clear and fresh in the mind as well; then one may quickly attain single-mindedness undisturbed — only when you have reached that state can you understand it. The Pure Land Dharma gate takes faith, vow, and practice as its purport and freedom from suffering and attainment of bliss as its wondrous function. One must give rise to the mind that welcomes the Pure Land and wearies of the Saha world, and then one will surely attain rebirth. Such an expedient Dharma gate — please do not be remiss; that is my hope.” Hearing his words and seeing his actions, there can be no doubt that at death, with single-mindedness undisturbed, he was born in the Western Pure Land.
Recorded by Ye Jinqian and Hong Wanchuan of the Pujing Lotus Society
